title: Gold: Digital Gold & Sovereign Gold Bonds
tagline: Gold's real role is a hedge and a diversifier, not a wealth engine. The modern ways to own it without lockers or making-charges — and the honest status of SGBs in 2026.
summary: Digital gold vs Gold ETFs vs Sovereign Gold Bonds, gold's role as a hedge, and the SGB situation today.

paragraphs: Indians love gold, but its job in a portfolio is widely misunderstood. Gold is a **hedge and diversifier**, not a primary growth asset. Over very long periods its returns roughly keep pace with inflation and tend to *trail* equity — but it often rises when stocks fall (crises, currency weakness, uncertainty), which smooths the overall ride.

So gold earns its place as a small slice (commonly **5–10%** of a portfolio) for stability, not as the main wealth engine. Physical jewellery, by the way, is a poor *investment*: you lose 8–25% to making charges and GST, and purity/storage are headaches.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Hold gold for diversification, capped at ~5–10% of your investments, and own it in a paper/digital form — never as jewellery bought 'as an investment'.

sections.title: The modern ways to own gold

blocks.title: Three paper-gold options
rows: App-bought gold stored by a vendor
Mutual-fund-style unit tracking gold price, in a Demat/fund
Govt bond denominated in grams of gold
No storage cost; no expense ratio
New issuances have effectively paused (see below)

paragraphs: **Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)** were historically the best way to own gold: issued by the RBI on behalf of the government, they pay **2.5% annual interest on top of gold's price movement**, have no storage cost, and — crucially — their **capital gains are completely tax-free if held to the 8-year maturity**. That combination beat every other form of gold.

blocks.title: Honest 2026 status of SGBs
blocks.text: The government has effectively stopped issuing NEW SGB tranches (no fresh issues since early 2024), as the scheme became expensive for them. So you usually can't buy a fresh SGB at issue today. You can still buy older SGBs on the stock exchange's secondary market — but they often trade at a premium and with thin liquidity. For most people now, a Gold ETF or gold fund is the practical default; digital gold is fine only for very small amounts.

paragraphs: Aarav is 22 with a tiny surplus and a 5-year car goal. **Gold should be a minor character in his story, if at all.** His priorities are the emergency fund and an equity index SIP for long-term growth. A small gold allocation (say ₹500/month into a gold ETF, or none at all) is optional diversification — not a substitute for the equity core.

blocks.text: A common beginner mistake is over-weighting gold because it 'feels safe' and familiar. But too much gold drags long-term returns versus equity. Keep it small and let equity do the heavy lifting while time is on your side.

cheatsheet: Gold is a hedge/diversifier, not a primary growth asset — cap it at ~5–10% of investments.
Physical jewellery is a poor investment (8–25% making charges + GST, storage/purity issues).
Own gold on paper: Digital Gold (small amounts), Gold ETF/fund (liquid, regulated), or SGBs.
SGBs historically best: +2.5% interest, no storage cost, tax-free gains if held to 8-yr maturity.
But new SGB tranches have effectively paused since early 2024 — buy older ones on the exchange (premium/illiquid) or use a Gold ETF as the practical default.
For a young investor, gold is optional and minor; the equity index core builds the wealth.

questions.prompt: Aarav's relative says 'gold only goes up, put most of your money there instead of risky shares.' What two things are wrong with this?
questions.hint: Consider gold's long-term return vs equity, and gold's actual role.
answer: First, gold does *not* only go up — it has long flat or falling stretches, and over long horizons it has generally **trailed equity**, roughly tracking inflation. Calling it a sure thing is wrong. Second, gold's role is a **hedge/diversifier**, not the main growth engine; over-weighting it drags long-term returns precisely when a 22-year-old should be maximising growth.
The right framing: keep gold a small slice (~5–10%) for stability, and let a low-cost equity index fund — which has the higher long-run return — do the heavy lifting for a multi-decade horizon.
keyPoints: Gold isn't a guaranteed riser; it has flat/down stretches

questions.prompt: Aarav wants some gold exposure and read that SGBs are the best way. What should he know before trying to buy one in 2026?
questions.hint: Are fresh SGBs being issued? What's the alternative?
answer: He should know that the government has effectively **stopped issuing new SGB tranches** (none since early 2024), so he generally can't subscribe to a fresh SGB at issue price today. He could buy older SGBs on the stock exchange's secondary market, but they often trade at a **premium with thin liquidity**, which erodes the advantage.

Given that, the practical default for a small, liquid gold allocation today is a **Gold ETF or gold fund**. Either way, he should keep gold a minor slice and prioritise his emergency fund and equity SIP first.
keyPoints: No new SGB tranches since early 2024
Gold ETF/fund is the practical default now
Keep gold small; equity core comes first
